energia.title: Energy
text:
In every electricity supply, two key concepts must be distinguished: POWER and ENERGY.
This will help us better understand what each concept represents within the electricity bill.
CONTRACTED POWER (CP)
What is it?
It is the fixed term on the bill.
In supplies above 15 kW, the contracted power is three-phase.
It represents the maximum electrical power capacity that can be requested at a given moment.
In other words: the amount of machinery that can operate simultaneously.
It mainly affects installations with 3.0TD and 6.1TD access tariffs:
— 3.0TD: power levels above 15 kW.
— 6.1TD: power levels above 450 kW.
In a three-phase system, the total power (kW) is divided among the three phases.
This allows higher electrical loads to be managed.
It is essential for industries, large companies, or homes with equipment such as elevators,
swimming pools, or garage doors.
CONSUMED ENERGY (CE)
What is it?
It is the variable term on the bill.
It represents the cost of the electricity actually consumed during the billing period.
It depends on how long the devices are operating.
It is calculated by multiplying the kWh consumed by the tariff's kWh price.
MAIN FEATURES
Load distribution:
Power is distributed across the three phases.
With digital meters, this distribution may be uneven depending on the needs.
Time periods and seasons:
Since June 2021 there have been 6 power periods (P1–P6) and 4 energy seasons.
The periods and seasons depend on the month and the tariff type.
Common voltages:
— Medium voltage (MV): 380–400 V.
— High voltage (HV): 1 kV to 30 kV.
It depends on the type of business.

calendari.title: Calendar
text:
TIME PERIODS AND SEASONS
Supplies above 15 kW (3.0TD, 6.1TD, MV and HV) use a billing structure
based on 6 time periods and 4 energy seasons.
Power is billed across the 6 periods regardless of the season, while energy
is billed according to the season in which it is consumed. This was the main regulatory change
included in CNMC Circular 3/2020 of January 15 and came into force in June 2021.
TIME PERIODS (P1 TO P6)
Each period has a different price and specific application hours.
— P1: High season. Months: December, January, February, and July.
— P2: High and medium-high seasons. In addition to the previous months, March and November.
— P3: Medium-high and medium seasons. March, November, June, August, and September.
— P4: Medium and low seasons. June, August, September, April, May, and October.
— P5: Low season: April, May, and October.
— P6: Common throughout the year.
For example, in December P1, P2, and P6 are billed. In March, P2, P3, and P6 are billed.
In June we have P3, P4, and P6. And in September P4, P5, and P6. The P6 period is common throughout the year.
And in some electricity retailers it is common to call them peak, flat, or valley instead of P1, P2, and P6.
PERIOD HOURS (PENINSULAR TIME)
P1: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P2: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P3: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P4: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P5: 08:00 to 09:00, from 14:00 to 18:00, and from 22:00 to 00:00.
P6: Weekends and public holidays (all day).
ENERGY SEASONS (CONSUMED ENERGY)
The season determines the price applied to periods P1 to P6.
There are 4 seasons: high, medium-high, medium, and low.
MONTHS BY SEASON
High season: January, February, July, December.
Medium-high season: March, June, October.
Medium season: April, May, November.
Low season: August, September.
HOW IS THIS APPLIED?
In 3.0TD and 6.1TD tariffs, periods P1 to P6 are applied equally, but with specific prices.
The P6 period is especially relevant in MV and HV due to its reduced tariff.
Companies can optimize costs by shifting consumption to P5 and P6.
SUMMARY
CP: 6 fixed periods each month.
Energy: or consumption. 4 seasons that vary depending on the month.
Each period has specific hours and a different price.

reactiva.title: Reactive
text:
REACTIVE ENERGY
Reactive energy is an “indirect” electrical consumption generated mainly by motors and
industrial equipment.
It does not perform useful work, but it overloads the installation and usually generates surcharges on the bill.
It is reduced with compensation equipment such as CAPACITOR BANKS, which act like an entry-only gate, allowing the necessary current to enter
but only using what the machine needs at that moment, while the rest is used by the installation.
In other words, when a machine starts up it generates a voltage peak, but does not use all of it
and sends part of it back to the grid, which is what is called 'gross energy'. Since it cannot be used, it is penalized
because that energy is lost. Some examples are freezers, elevators, cold storage rooms, etc.
PHOTOVOLTAICS AND SURPLUS COMPENSATION:
Photovoltaic panels are what generate these surpluses:
There are times when we do not consume all the energy produced by our installation, such as during holidays.
or during a season of lower production, our PV system will continue producing for self-consumption, but part of that production will not be consumed.
In this situation, our PV system generates surpluses.
And surpluses are the energy PRODUCED BUT NOT CONSUMED that is returned to the grid
and compensated according to electricity market conditions with regulated limitations.
Photovoltaic installations are usually sized mainly to cover
their own consumption, and oversizing them solely to generate surpluses is generally not very profitable
and is subject to technical and regulatory limitations, such as connection point capacity.
